editorial.intro: An independent parametric garment-system exploration connecting body measurements, garment construction and exportable pattern geometry.
editorial.introFa: کاوش مستقل یک سیستم پارامتریک پوشاک برای اتصال اندازه‌های بدن، کالیبراسیون الگو و خروجی DXF قابل استفاده در CLO 3D.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PROJECT CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: Exploring a parametric garment workflow
caseStudy.body: Veblen is an independent concept project exploring how body measurements and adjustable garment parameters can be connected in a digital pattern workflow. It is a design and technical exploration, not a production-deployed product.

caseStudy.label: 02 / PROBLEM FRAMING
caseStudy.title: Make body measurements translate into usable pattern geometry
caseStudy.body: The central challenge was to connect body reference points, measurement inputs and garment construction logic in a way that could be calibrated and exported, rather than leaving the system as a visual-only 3D concept.

caseStudy.label: 03 / CALIBRATION & COLLABORATION
caseStudy.title: Test the system with pattern-making expertise
caseStudy.body: I ran multiple calibration tests on one pattern and worked with two pattern makers, who were involved and informed during the exploration. Their pattern-making knowledge helped ground the technical direction in garment-construction requirements.

caseStudy.label: 04 / TECHNICAL DECISION
caseStudy.title: Treat export as part of the design workflow
caseStudy.body: The system generated DXF output intended for use in CLO 3D. This connected the parametric exploration to a downstream garment-visualisation workflow, rather than ending at an on-screen preview.

caseStudy.label: 05 / VALIDATION EVIDENCE
caseStudy.title: Documented reference geometry and export checks
caseStudy.body: The project documentation records seven body-measurement reference points, a maximum 0.03% deviation for the size-M reference avatar geometry, and zero structural errors in the documented DXF/SVG validation. These figures describe specific documented checks, not universal fit accuracy across body types.

caseStudy.label: 06 / DESIGN OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: A technically grounded concept with a downstream file output
caseStudy.body: Veblen brought body representation, parametric calibration, pattern-maker input and DXF export into one exploration. The output was suitable for the intended CLO 3D workflow; this case study does not claim production adoption or validation across all sizes and body types.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Independent Product Designer · Creative Technology
caseStudy.body: Concept direction, product-interface exploration, calibration work and collaboration with two pattern makers. Independent project, 2025–2026.

impact.label: DOCUMENTED TECHNICAL EVIDENCE
impact.title: From body references to exportable geometry
impact.note: Figures are limited to specific project documentation and tests; they are not generalised fit-accuracy claims.
impact.foot: Calibration involved one pattern and two pattern makers. The project is an independent concept exploration, not a production deployment.

editorial.intro: An employee experience platform connecting survey creation, feedback and people analytics.
editorial.introFa: پلتفرم تجربه‌ی کارکنان برای ساخت نظرسنجی، دریافت بازخورد و تحلیل داده‌های منابع انسانی.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PRODUCT CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: Employee feedback needed to lead somewhere
caseStudy.body: Pulse Check is an employee experience platform built from zero, shipped and used in production. It connected survey creation and employee feedback with a path for HR teams to interpret findings and act on them.

caseStudy.label: 02 / PROBLEM FRAMING
caseStudy.title: A dashboard full of numbers is not the same as an actionable insight
caseStudy.body: The product challenge was not simply to display survey results. HR needed to understand what a signal meant, why it mattered, who should respond and whether an action changed the next measurement.

caseStudy.label: 03 / REJECTED DIRECTION
caseStudy.title: Avoid stopping at static reports
caseStudy.body: The product direction moved beyond a conventional reporting dashboard or a screen filled with disconnected metrics. Instead, the experience was structured around the full lifecycle of an insight, from the question that produced feedback to the action taken in response.

caseStudy.label: 04 / EXPERIENCE MODEL
caseStudy.title: Connect survey, signal, priority and action
caseStudy.body: The experience links survey creation, supported survey frameworks, measurable indices, heatmaps, priority mapping and insight cards. An insight can carry response evidence and raw comments, then be assigned an owner, an action and a deadline.

caseStudy.label: 05 / CLOSE THE LOOP
caseStudy.title: Make follow-through part of the product
caseStudy.body: An action tracker represents proposed, in-progress and completed actions, with re-measurement in the next survey cycle. The intention is to keep an insight alive after the report is read, rather than leaving it as a static observation.

caseStudy.label: 06 / DESIGN OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: From collecting feedback to giving an insight a life
caseStudy.body: The shipped product connects quantitative patterns and qualitative evidence to ownership and follow-through. Six survey frameworks are supported in the documented product. Sample dashboard values shown in portfolio screens are demo data and are not presented as company results.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Product Designer · primary design ownership
caseStudy.body: I led product design within a two-person design team; the second designer mainly contributed feedback and critique. The project sits within my Jobvision employment period, November 2023–April 2025; exact project dates are not separately confirmed.

impact.label: PRODUCT DESIGN OUTCOME
impact.title: Give an insight a life beyond the report
impact.note: Capabilities documented in the product experience. Sample dashboard figures are illustrative and are not real company outcomes.

metrics.detail: Track action and review the next cycle

impact.foot: The product was shipped and used in production. No actual participation, favorability, eNPS or improvement figures are claimed from demo screens.

editorial.intro: A travel platform connecting destination discovery, trip planning, local recommendations and access to people who know the place.
editorial.introFa: پلتفرم برنامه‌ریزی سفر برای کشف مقصد، تخمین هزینه و مسافت، پیشنهادهای محلی و ارتباط با افراد بومی.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PROJECT ORIGIN
caseStudy.title: The questions that begin after booking
caseStudy.body: Iran Unseen started from my own experience of spending three months in Yerevan. Through conversations with people there, I noticed how many practical questions travelers have about everyday local life—payments, shopping, places to visit and experiences that typical booking platforms rarely explain.

caseStudy.label: 02 / PROBLEM FRAMING
caseStudy.title: A destination is not the same as understanding a place
caseStudy.body: Traditional travel platforms often help people choose and book a destination, but leave much of the local context unanswered. Travelers may still feel uncertain about how things work, what is worth exploring nearby, and who they can safely ask for guidance.

caseStudy.label: 03 / PRODUCT DIRECTION
caseStudy.title: Bring the human and local layer into trip planning
caseStudy.body: I shaped Iran Unseen around a broader journey: choose a destination, understand the trip, discover relevant options around it, and request a connection with someone local. The goal is to make the experience more informed and human before the traveler arrives.

caseStudy.label: 04 / TRIP PLANNING
caseStudy.title: Turn a destination into a set of useful next steps
caseStudy.body: The implemented experience includes destination selection, distance and estimated trip-cost information, plus contextual suggestions and offers for additional options around the selected destination and along the journey.

caseStudy.label: 05 / LOCAL PARTICIPATION
caseStudy.title: Design both sides of the local connection
caseStudy.body: Travelers can submit a request to connect with a local. A separate registration experience is also designed for locals who want to join the platform and receive offers. Requests currently reach the project owner by email; the request path is implemented, but this should not be presented as a scaled, automated local marketplace.

caseStudy.label: 06 / DESIGN OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: A usable travel-planning platform, beyond destination booking
caseStudy.body: The live product brings destination choice, distance and cost estimation, contextual recommendations, local-request submission and local onboarding into one experience. The project has no confirmed user or booking metrics yet, so its outcome is described through implemented capabilities rather than adoption claims.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Independent product design and implementation
caseStudy.body: Independent project. Product concept, experience structure and interface design across traveler planning and local registration journeys. Exact project dates remain to be confirmed.

impact.label: PRODUCT CAPABILITIES / IMPLEMENTED EXPERIENCE
impact.title: From choosing a place to feeling prepared for it
impact.note: These are implemented product capabilities, not user-growth or booking-performance metrics.

metrics.detail: Offers and options around the destination
Traveler can submit a request to a local
A separate registration experience for locals

impact.foot: Local requests currently arrive by email to the project owner. The implemented request flow is not represented as a scaled automated marketplace.

editorial.intro: An ATS dashboard designed to help HR teams see recruitment work, candidate status and priorities in one operational view.
editorial.introFa: داشبورد ATS برای اینکه تیم منابع انسانی وضعیت استخدام، متقاضیان و اولویت‌های کاری را در یک نمای عملیاتی ببیند.

caseStudy.label: 01 / THE PROBLEM
caseStudy.title: Recruitment work was scattered across spreadsheets and reports
caseStudy.body: HR teams were relying on Excel and fragmented information to follow recruitment work. Tasks, candidate statuses and reporting were spread across different places, making it difficult to understand what needed attention first.

caseStudy.label: 02 / FIELD INPUT
caseStudy.title: Designing alongside the people doing the work
caseStudy.body: I worked directly with HR staff, listened to their feedback and iterated on the dashboard around the information they needed to see. Their feedback exposed missing candidate context in the first-view overview and made prioritisation a central requirement.

caseStudy.label: 03 / REJECTED DIRECTION
caseStudy.title: Separate report pages would preserve the fragmentation
caseStudy.body: I explored the idea of giving each report its own page, but moved away from it. That approach would keep HR moving between separate views instead of helping them understand the state of recruitment from one place.

caseStudy.label: 04 / DESIGN DECISION
caseStudy.title: Bring the operational picture into one dashboard
caseStudy.body: The chosen direction combined data visualisation, task tracking, reminders, status labels and prioritisation in a single overview. The intent was to make the most important information visible without requiring HR to assemble it manually from multiple reports.

caseStudy.label: 05 / WORKFLOW CLARITY
caseStudy.title: Make overdue work and candidate status easier to recognise
caseStudy.body: Clear labels made overdue tasks easier to identify. Candidate status information that HR had said was missing was brought into the initial overview, while priority cues helped users understand what needed attention.

caseStudy.label: 06 / OBSERVED OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: More engagement and positive feedback—without invented percentages
caseStudy.body: The user recalls that analytics showed increased engagement with the dashboard and that HR feedback was positive. They also recall a substantial improvement in the speed of managing HR tasks, but no exact before-and-after timing or analytics figures are available. These observations are reported qualitatively, not converted into a fabricated percentage.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Product Designer · ATS dashboard and mobile presentation
caseStudy.body: My scope was the ATS dashboard and its mobile presentation, not the wider ATS product or every recruitment workflow. The design was informed by direct collaboration and feedback from HR staff. Project dates are not separately confirmed; shown within the Jobvision employment period, November 2023–April 2025.

impact.label: OBSERVED DESIGN OUTCOME
impact.title: From scattered reporting to one operational view
impact.note: Qualitative evidence from HR collaboration and product analytics; exact numerical deltas are not available.

metrics.detail: Data, tasks, reminders and statuses together
Clear labels make late tasks easier to spot
Missing context added to the first-view overview
Analytics showed more engagement; no exact figure retained

impact.foot: HR feedback was positive and task handling felt substantially faster to the user, but no measured time saving or percentage is claimed.

editorial.intro: An AI creative workspace presented across desktop, Persian-language and mobile interfaces.
editorial.introFa: فضای خلاقیت مبتنی بر هوش مصنوعی در نسخه‌های دسکتاپ، فارسی و موبایل.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PROJECT CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: One workspace. Multiple creative capabilities.
caseStudy.body: Humaani is an AI creative workspace bringing creative tools and related workflows into one product environment. The design task was to make that breadth feel like a coherent workspace.

caseStudy.label: 02 / PROBLEM FRAMING
caseStudy.title: The challenge was connection, not just individual screens.
caseStudy.body: Distinct capabilities needed a shared structure. Without clear relationships between modules, navigation and user journeys, the workspace could feel like a collection of separate tools.

caseStudy.label: 03 / EXPERIENCE ARCHITECTURE
caseStudy.title: Map the product before polishing the interface.
caseStudy.body: I worked on the information architecture, navigation hierarchy and cross-module flows, organising how the different parts of the workspace relate and how users move between them.

caseStudy.label: 04 / SYSTEM DESIGN
caseStudy.title: Create consistency that can scale across modules.
caseStudy.body: I developed a shared design system and reusable interface patterns to establish consistent visual and interaction rules across the product, rather than treating each area as a separate design problem.

caseStudy.label: 05 / EXPERIENCE ADAPTATION
caseStudy.title: One product language across two languages and screens.
caseStudy.body: The experience was designed for Persian and English, with responsive mobile layouts. The work considered language direction, hierarchy and layout adaptation as part of the product experience.

caseStudy.label: 06 / DESIGN OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: A more coherent foundation for an AI workspace.
caseStudy.body: The resulting design connects product structure, navigation, interface patterns and responsive bilingual experiences. This describes the delivered design scope—not a claim of measured business or usability uplift.

impact.label: DESIGN IMPACT / SCOPE AT A GLANCE
impact.title: The footprint of the design work
impact.note: Verified project-scope indicators. These are not conversion, retention or usability performance metrics.
impact.foot: Impact is expressed through the design foundation delivered: connected architecture, consistent interface patterns and a bilingual, responsive workspace—not through invented outcome statistics.

editorial.intro: An executive talent platform, with design focused on the candidate-side experience from profile discovery to contact.
editorial.introFa: پلتفرم استعدادهای مدیریتی با تمرکز طراحی بر تجربه کاندیدا؛ از معرفی و کشف پروفایل تا ارتباط.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PRODUCT CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: A more discreet route into executive opportunities
caseStudy.body: Mirana is a Jobvision-group executive talent and headhunting service. Unlike a conventional job-board journey, its proposition includes relevant senior opportunities and a more discreet path for candidates to be discovered and contacted.

caseStudy.label: 02 / DESIGN SCOPE
caseStudy.title: The candidate experience was my responsibility
caseStudy.body: My design scope covered the candidate side only. I worked across talent profiles, search and discovery, the contact journey and the mobile experience. The employer-side panel and workflows were outside my scope.

caseStudy.label: 03 / PROFILE EXPERIENCE
caseStudy.title: Give professional context room to speak
caseStudy.body: The candidate-facing experience needed to present senior talent and profile information in a way that supports discovery and helps people understand the opportunity to engage, without reducing the journey to a generic job listing.

caseStudy.label: 04 / DISCOVERY & CONTACT
caseStudy.title: Connect being found with the next step
caseStudy.body: I designed the search and discovery surfaces alongside the contact flow, keeping profile exploration and the next action connected. This creates a candidate-side journey from being represented on the platform to receiving or responding to relevant contact.

caseStudy.label: 05 / MOBILE EXPERIENCE
caseStudy.title: Keep the candidate journey coherent on mobile
caseStudy.body: The mobile experience was part of the design scope, extending the profile and contact journey to a narrower, on-the-go context.

caseStudy.label: 06 / DESIGN OUTCOME
caseStudy.title: A connected candidate-side talent experience
caseStudy.body: The designed scope connects profile presentation, search and discovery, contact and mobile use. The user recalls substantial traffic arriving from Jobvision, but no reliable user count is available; no adoption, contact-conversion or hiring-placement metric is claimed.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Product Designer · candidate-side experience
caseStudy.body: Product design across candidate profiles, search and discovery, contact flow and mobile experience. Employer panel and employer workflows were not part of my design scope. Project dates are not separately confirmed; shown within the Jobvision employment period, November 2023–April 2025.

impact.label: DESIGN SCOPE / CANDIDATE EXPERIENCE
impact.title: A connected path for executive talent
impact.note: The focus areas describe the work owned by the designer, not measured hiring or platform outcomes.

metrics.detail: A clear path to initiate contact

impact.foot: Employer-side product design is explicitly excluded. Traffic volume and recruitment outcomes are not quantified.

editorial.intro: An FMCG marketplace spanning customer shopping, store operations, shopper workflows, product information and reporting.
editorial.introFa: بازارگاه کالاهای تندمصرف با تجربه خرید مشتری، عملیات فروشگاه، جریان Shopper، اطلاعات محصول و گزارش‌ها.

caseStudy.label: 01 / PRODUCT CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: A marketplace connecting shoppers and local stores
caseStudy.body: Pinket was an online grocery and FMCG marketplace with customer-facing shopping and operational tools for stores and shoppers. My work took place before a later company pivot toward a broader store-data platform.

caseStudy.label: 02 / DESIGN SCOPE
caseStudy.title: Working across the marketplace, not just one screen
caseStudy.body: My design contribution covered almost all of the main product areas I was involved with: the customer shopping journey, store dashboard and operations, shopper and product-selection experience, product information and reporting.

caseStudy.label: 03 / MULTI-SIDED EXPERIENCE
caseStudy.title: Different users, different jobs to be done
caseStudy.body: The product connected customer decisions, shopper execution and store operations. Each side needed its own information hierarchy and actions, while still belonging to one marketplace experience.

caseStudy.label: 04 / OPERATIONAL DESIGN
caseStudy.title: Make store and shopper information usable
caseStudy.body: The design work included operational dashboards, shopper-related views, product information and reporting. These surfaces supported the people managing and fulfilling the marketplace experience, alongside the customer shopping flow.

caseStudy.label: 05 / CUSTOMER JOURNEY
caseStudy.title: Keep the shopping experience connected to fulfilment
caseStudy.body: The customer-facing journey was part of the same design scope as the operational tools. This made it possible to consider the marketplace as a connected service rather than treating the app and store-side tools as unrelated products.

caseStudy.label: 06 / SCALE CONTEXT
caseStudy.title: An early-stage product with roughly 300–1,000 monthly users
caseStudy.body: I remember Pinket having approximately 300–1,000 monthly users during my time there. This is a retrospective estimate, not a verified analytics export, and it describes product scale rather than growth caused by my design work.

caseStudy.label: 07 / ROLE & SCOPE
caseStudy.title: UI/UX Designer · two-person design team
caseStudy.body: I worked across the main customer and operational product areas as part of a two-person design team. Employment period: January 2022–June 2023. A later pivot to a Tehran-wide store-data platform happened after my involvement and is not presented as an outcome of my work.

impact.label: PRODUCT CONTEXT / DESIGN SCOPE
impact.title: A multi-sided marketplace at an early stage
impact.note: Monthly user count is a personal retrospective estimate, not a verified analytics figure or attributable design result.
impact.foot: Two-person design team. Later company pivot and subsequent platform scale are outside this case study’s scope.
